t: Longest Alternating Subarray After Removing At Most One Element
o: An alternating subarray's adjacent comparisons strictly alternate between up and down. Without removal, the answer is the longest alternating run. Removal helps only when it splices an alternating segment ending just before the removed element with one starting just after it, provided the comparison bridging the gap continues the alternation. In Example 1 no removal is needed (whole array alternates, length 4). In Example 2, removing index 3 lets the length-1 segment [1] merge with the length-3 segment [3,2,1] to reach 4. Example 3 shows equal neighbors break everything, giving 1. With n up to 1e5 we need an O(n) sweep, not rechecking all subarrays.
k: Precompute, for each index, the longest alternating run ending there (with its last comparison sign) and starting there (with its first comparison sign).
Removing element p can only help by merging the run ending at p-1 with the run starting at p+1 across the bridge comparison nums[p+1] vs nums[p-1].

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force with removal enumeration
a.i: For each candidate removal index (and no removal), scan all subarrays of the resulting array and track the longest alternating one. Straightforward but quadratic or worse.
s: For each choice of removed index p in {-1} ∪ {0..n-1}: build the remaining array.
For each start, extend while comparisons keep alternating.
a.t: O(n^3) — n removal choices times quadratic subarray scanning; fine only for tiny inputs.

a.n: Approach 2: Precomputed run lengths with bridge merging (optimal)
a.i: endL[i]/endS[i] give the longest alternating run ending at i and its last comparison sign; startL[i]/startS[i] give the same from the right. Any alternating subarray ending at p-1 with length > 1 is a suffix of the maximal run there, so it shares endS — checking only the maximal runs at each bridge p is sufficient. The no-removal answer is max(endL).
s: Sweep left to right filling endL/endS: extend when the new comparison sign is nonzero and opposite the previous sign.
Sweep right to left filling startL/startS analogously.
For each interior p, let a = sign(nums[p+1] - nums[p-1]); if a != 0, endS[p-1] != a (or endL[p-1] = 1) and startS[p+1] == a (or startL[p+1] = 1), candidate endL[p-1] + startL[p+1].
a.t: O(n) — three linear passes (two sweeps plus one bridge scan).
a.sp: O(n) for the four auxiliary arrays.

w: Present the run-length precomputation as the main solution; the brute force is only for building intuition. Pitfalls: equal adjacent elements (sign 0) breaking runs, off-by-one at the array boundary when p-1 or p+1 does not exist, and remembering that a length-1 side imposes no sign constraint. Follow-ups: remove at most m elements (generalize the bridge to m gaps), or count alternating subarrays instead.
